title: Phoneme Choir — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Phoneme Choir's rich face: the two lessons the build learned, each made playable and tested — the lag before a word in four voices, trimmed and measured on the build's own samples, and the trill that never came, re-rendered and measured past the spelling. I grow when the entry is enriched again; I never hold the entry's words.

verdicts.why: A real test that could have gone the other way: the trill symbol handed straight to the model reads a longest run of 1 against 6–8 for the modelled flutter, and the ruler reads 5 at 25.8 a second on a real recorded trill (Commons), so its no means something; walks up ruler → one spelling → six → the door. Note: cite 'close to 30 a second' (Ladefoged, Cochran & Disner 1977, 26–32 Hz).

verdicts.file: Phoneme Choir — rich — same word, four voices.html
verdicts.why: Runs the build's own onset rule on the build's own files (347/352 exact, recomputed independently) and walks one breath → onset → four voices → trim → twelve keys; its test found the trim aligns where sound starts, not where the word gets loud, and holds that as offer 2 rather than changing the text.

pieces.near: Repeated-letter strings get parsed as character sequences
pieces.title: the spelling is the prompt · four steps
pieces.caption: **The trill audition, re-rendered and measured.** A ruler first: Kokoro’s brah with a modelled flutter, read as dips in a row at 20 to 45 a second. Then brrrrahhh as the model was handed it, phonemes from kokoro-onnx’s espeak-ng front end that read the letters by name (B, R, R, R, rah). Then the six other spellings, ssssss and ahhh in a row. Last, the door around the spelling: the trill symbol handed straight to the model, in two voices, and still no flutter. The renders are new (the audition files did not survive), made 2026-11-03 with the build’s settings. The ruler says yes to a real trill: run on a recorded alveolar trill (Wikimedia Commons, Alveolar_trill.ogg) it finds 5 dips in a row at 25.8 a second, so its no on Kokoro means something; real trills run close to 30 a second (26–32 Hz, Ladefoged, Cochran and Disner 1977; two or three taps, Ladefoged and Maddieson 1996, p. 218). Kokoro's three Spanish voices, whose language trills, reached a longest run of 2 (the challenger's check, not in the piece).

pieces.near: Without per-file detection, the keyboard would feel inconsistently sluggish
pieces.title: same word, four voices · five steps
pieces.caption: **The lag before the word, on the build’s own samples.** One knock and its 138 ms of breath; the build’s onset rule, run in the page and agreeing with offsets.json; the four voices of knock that the build’s audition.sfz loaded, untrimmed and then trimmed; and last, twelve keys in all four layers with how soon each gets loud after the key, trim off and on, by a ruler you can move. The trim lines up where every voice starts; where the word gets loud still differs by voice on most keys.

offers.what: Kokoro syllabifies repeated consonants: the mechanism is kokoro-onnx’s espeak-ng front end, which reads an unknown string as letter names — brrrrahhh → /bˌiːˌɑːɹɹˌɑːɹɹˈɑːɹɹˈɑː/, B R R R rah; ssssss → six “ess”, as the page guessed. Two refinements: the prompt is not only the spelling, since kokoro-onnx takes phonemes directly (is_phonemes=True), but handed the trill symbol r in three strings, am_adam and af_bella still made no flutter (longest run of dips 1, against 6 and 8 for a modelled 28 Hz flutter, and 5 for a recorded real trill); and held vowels shrink rather than syllabify — ahhh becomes one /ˈɑː/, uuuuh two /ˈuːuː/. The renders are made, not gathered (the audition files did not survive), labelled origin: made, and reproduce byte-identical from the tracked render script.

Per-file onset detection: the numbers hold (onsets 22.9–217.9 ms, median 54.6; knock 137.75 ms in bf_isabella, 31.25 in am_puck; the page’s rule reproduces offsets.json exactly for 347 of 352 files, the rest within 3 samples; recomputed independently by the challenger). Line 84, “every key fires immediately into the percussive transient regardless of voice”, is true of where sound starts: every file starts 1 ms after its first 5 ms above −30 dBFS. Line 89, “so we land on the transient peak”, is false: the key starts a median 98.5 ms before the file’s loudest 5 ms. Over all 88 keys a key’s four voices reach 20 dB under their loudest 5.7 ms apart with the trim (79.7 without), but 10 dB under 59.9 ms apart (99.8 without); only 5 keys, knock among them, land within 10 ms there. Suggest: every key starts its sound at once, whatever the voice; how soon the word gets loud after that still varies by voice. Which ruler matches the felt beat wants an ear.
